summary: Explains how devices on an ATM network can use ILMI to automatically learn the ATM address of a MARS server, which helps with multicast, without manual configuration.

plainLanguage.summary: A new student asks the front desk where to find the group-message office. The network switch tells the device where to go.

questions: how to find a mars server
how does ilmi find a mars server
what is the service registry mib
how do diskless hosts find a mars server
subtitle: How an ATM host or router asks its switch where the MARS multicast server is, instead of being configured by hand.

tldr.problem: Using MARS normally means statically configuring at least one ATM address on every host or router, which is cumbersome and error-prone and rules out diskless hosts.
tldr.mechanism: The host queries the Service Registry MIB on its ATM switch over ILMI, using SNMP GetNext, and reads the ATM address of the MARS server from the matching table row.
tldr.outcome: Clients with no local configuration can find a MARS server, and redundant servers are supported by ordering rows by index. Servers themselves are still configured locally.

today: RFC 2602 is a Proposed Standard from June 1999 and, per the metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated. A companion document, RFC 2601, applies the same method to ATMARP servers.

sections.title: Why Server Discovery Is Needed
sections.content:
Setting up a host or router to use MARS (defined in RFC 2022) is described as cumbersome and error-prone. It requires at least one ATM address to be statically configured on each host or router in the network.

That also makes a diskless host that uses MARS impossible, since local configuration is required. ILMI-based Server Discovery, called simply server discovery in the memo, solves both problems by letting the device ask the network for the server address.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of writing the address of the group-message office on every student's hand, each student asks the front desk on arrival.

sections.title: ILMI and Its Sides of the Link
sections.content:
The Integrated Local Management Interface (ILMI) lets ATM-attached devices such as hosts, routers and ATM switches exchange management information. It is based on SNMP version 1 and supports get, get-next, set and trap operations.

ILMI calls the switch side of an ATM link the network side and the host or router side the user side. The Service Registry MIB is implemented on the network side and queried from the user side.
sections.plainLanguage: The switch is the front desk and the host is the visitor. The visitor asks and the desk answers from its list.

sections.title: The Service Registry Table
sections.content:
Server discovery uses the Service Registry MIB from ILMI Specification Version 4.0. ATM switches must support it to support the existing framework for IP over ATM, as embodied by ATMARP and MARS. Each row of the service registry table has five fields.

  • atmfSrvcRegPort: the ATM port the entry is about. Zero may be used for the interface over which the request arrived.
  • atmfSrvcRegServiceID: an object identifier naming the type of service.
  • atmfSrvcRegATMAddress: the full address of the service, which the client uses to connect to it.
  • atmfSrvcRegAddressIndex: an arbitrary integer separating rows for the same service on the same port.
  • atmfSrvcRegParm1: an octet string whose size and meaning depend on the service ID.

The table is indexed by port, service ID and address index. For MARS, the service ID is atmfSrvcRegMARS, which is 1.3.6.1.4.1.353.1.5.4. It names no managed objects and is only used to find the right rows.
sections.plainLanguage: The front desk keeps a list with a row for each helper: what kind it is, where to find it, and a number to tell similar ones apart.

sections.title: The MARS Parameter String
sections.content:
For MARS, the atmfSrvcRegParm1 string follows the field names used in RFC 2022. In order: mar$pro.type (16 bits, protocol type), mar$pro.snap (40 bits, an optional extension to the protocol type), mar$plen (8 bits, protocol address length), mar$addr (network address, plen octets) and mar$mask (network mask, plen octets).

Address and mask are in network byte order. IPv4 uses type 0x0800 and length 4, and IPv6 uses 0x86DD and length 16. For both IPv4 and IPv6 the SNAP extension is 0.
sections.plainLanguage: Each row also says which network the helper serves, like a sign reading 'this office is for Room 5 only'.

sections.title: How a MARS Client Finds a Server
sections.content:
The client uses the SNMP GetNext operator to sweep (a linear search) the service registry table. It starts at port 0, the MARS service ID and index 0, holding the port and service ID constant.

A client with no local configuration, such as a diskless workstation, must use the row with the lowest index if several servers are listed. A client with local IP configuration must use a row that has the appropriate IP address. In the RFC's example, a router with interfaces 1.0.0.1/8, 128.10.0.1/16 and 171.69.150.226/24 looks for three different atmfSrvcRegParm1 values, one per network.

Once it finds the right row, the client may set up an SVC to that server and carry on with ordinary MARS operations.

Redundancy uses several rows. The primary server has the lowest index, and the client must try the primary before a secondary. Administrators must make sure the listed servers are synchronized.
sections.plainLanguage: The visitor reads down the list until they find the line for their own room, and goes to the first helper listed. If that one is away, they try the next.

sections.title: Server Behavior and PNNI Augmented Routing
sections.content:
A MARS server is configured locally. It may read the registry data to check it, and if it finds an incorrect row it may flag the error in a locally significant way.

The ATM Forum has also developed PNNI Augmented Routing (PAR), which can distribute data such as MARS server addresses, and is developing Proxy PAR for UNI-attached hosts. The memo says these offer a promising way to manage the registry tables, and need no change to this mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: The helper still gets told its job by hand. Later the school may find a smarter way to keep the front desk's list current, and visitors would ask the same way.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The mechanism relies on the security of the ILMI management framework. Access to user-side and network-side information is controlled by MIB design, not by protocol security mechanisms.

The Service Registry MIB is read-only. Any user-side device may query it but cannot change it over ILMI. The table must be changed by local configuration on the ATM switch.
sections.plainLanguage: Visitors can read the front desk's list but cannot write on it. Only the staff can change it.
